chapter: Minton's, Louis Armstrong and the South
title: Dizzy spreads the style while Clarke is in the army
summary: Dizzy understood Clarke's ideas from birth and taught others to play like him while Clarke was drafted, just after he had led Kenny Clarke's Kansas City Six featuring Coleman Hawkins.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: And after the style had really caught on, when -- well, how it really -- Dizzy knew all the fundamentals. He knew exactly what I was doing.
Yeah. Because he'd seen you building.
Yeah, that's right. He saw it from its birth.
And when I was drafted into the Army, well then Diz began teaching drums.
He was teaching everybody to play like Kenny Clarke. Man you've got to play that -- that's not the way it goes. Like he taught Art Blakey, Max --

And Dizzy knew -- he knew exactly -- just like he caught the drift of Chano Pozo (PHONETIC). He understood immediately what Chano Pozo was doing. And right now he can play the congas as good as anyone I know.
Oh, sometimes I'd rather have Dizzy play congas than any Cuban or anybody else.
Really. Because he has a -- a fantastic comprehension of rhythm.
That's what makes him such a wonderful trumpet player. That's what made Lester Young such a wonderful saxophone player.
And Bird. It was that conception of rhythm.
And I think that's the whole thing. What Diz used to do -- I used to do things that he would put notes to what I was doing. That's how fascinated with rhythm he was. Can you imagine that?
And when I went in the army --
Yeah. He would put notes to these -- just the rhythm things that I would do. And when I went into the army, when Diz took over. When I came back everyone was
It's funny isn't it. Life is very funny, because it's funny you had to go into the army when you'd broken the ground and introduced this.
Just when I had my name on 52nd Street.
Kenny Clarke's Kansas City Six, featuring Coleman Hawkins.
Just when I was figuring, well --
Well, we're jumping ahead a little too fast.
Because we're still back there, at Minton's.
